paragraphs.text: As thou seemest willing to do, and for very good reason. {Jer 2:22-24} Thou art but a beaten rebel, and to stand it out with me is to no purpose; thou must either turn or burn. Neither will it help thee to return fainly, for I love truth in the inward parts, and hate hypocrisy, halting, and tepidity. If therefore thou wilt return,
paragraphs.anchor: If thou wilt return, O Israel.

paragraphs.text: Return as far as to me; not from one evil course to another, {Jer 2:36} for that is but to be tossed as a ball from one of the devil’s hands to the other, but "to me with thy whole heart," seriously, sincerely, and zealously; for Non amat, qui non zelat. To a tyrant thou shalt not turn, but to one that will both assist thee, {Pro 1:23} and accept thee. {Zec 1:2}
paragraphs.anchor: Return unto me.

paragraphs.text: i.e., Thine idols out of thine house and out of thine heart. {Eze 14:3-4}
paragraphs.anchor: And if thou wilt put away thine abominations out of my sight

paragraphs.text: But still dwell in the land and do good; feeding on faith, as Tremellius rendereth that Psa 37:3.
paragraphs.anchor: Then shalt thou not remove.

paragraphs.text: Not by Baal shalt thou swear, or other idols, but by the living God, or by the life of God. The Egyptians once sware by the life of Pharaoh, as the proud Spaniards now do by the life of their king. But, to speak properly, none liveth but the Lord, and none should be sworn by but he alone, an oath being a proof of the divine power, which one worshippeth. The Pythagoreans used to swear by πεπρακτην, Quaternity, which they called παγαν αενναου φυσεως, the fountain of eternal being; and this doubtless was the same with τετραγραμματον, Jehovah.
paragraphs.anchor: And thou shalt swear, The Lord liveth.

paragraphs.text: Vere, rite, et iuste: {a} (1.) In truth, {Rom 9:1} that is, to that which is true, lest we fall into perjury. {Lev 19:12} And (2.) Truly, agreeable both to the intentions of our mind, not deceitfully, {Psa 24:2} and agreeable also to the intentions of him that ministereth the oath, and not with mental reservations, as Romish priests oft swear.
paragraphs.anchor: In truth, in judgment, and in righteousness.

paragraphs.text: Or, Considerately, duly weighing the conditions and circumstances, not rashly and unadvisedly, {Lev 5:4 1Sa 14:39} as those that swear in heat and choler, swear when they should fear. {Deu 10:20; Deu 28:58} The Romans used that most considerate word arbitror, when the jurors said those things which they knew most certainly. {b} The Grecians, when they would swear by their Jupiter, out of the mere dread and reverence of his name, forbore to mention him. And the Egyptians bore such respect to Mercurius Trismegistus, that they held it not lawful to pronounce his name lightly and rashly. This is check to many swearing pseudo-Christians. Such also as swear in jest, will, without repentance, go to hell in earnest. The ancient form of taking and imposing an oath was, Give glory to God. {Jos 7:19 Joh 9:24}
paragraphs.anchor: In judgment.

paragraphs.text: (1.) Promising by oath lawful and possible things only, not making an oath a bond of iniquity. {1Sa 25:21-22; 1Sa 28:10} (2.) Careful to perform what we have sworn, though to our own hindrance. {Psa 15:4}
paragraphs.anchor: And in righteousness.

paragraphs.text: Or, Shall be blessed in him - that is, in that God to whom thou returnest, and by whom thou thus swearest. They shall turn to God by thine example, and hold themselves happy in such a good turn.
paragraphs.anchor: And the nations shall bless themselves in him.

paragraphs.text: {a} Tremel.
{b} Suidas.

Novellate vobis novale. Tertullian rendereth it, Renovate vobis novamen novuum, put off the old man, and put on the new. See Hos 10:11. {See Trapp on "Hos 10:11"} By the practice of repentance, runcate, extirpate, root up and rid your hearts and lives of all vile lusts and vicious practices. The breaking up of sinful hearts may prevent the breaking down of a sinful nation.
paragraphs.anchor: Break up your fallow ground.

paragraphs.text: i.e., Cares and lusts of life, fitly called thorns, because (1.) They prick and gore the soul; (2.) Harbour the old serpent; (3.) Choke the word. There is no looking for a harvest in a hedge: stock them, and stub them up therefore; {1Pe 2:1 Jas 1:21} do not plough here, and make a trench there, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: Sow not among thorns

paragraphs.text: There is a twofold circumcision, corporis et cordis, outward and inward: that without this availeth nothing. {Gal 6:15} See the inward described Col 2:11. It is the putting off the old Adam with his actions. It is purgatio animae et aliectio vitiorum, saith Origen; the cleansing of the soul, and the casting away of sin, that filthy foreskin, that "superfluity of naughtiness." {Jas 1:21} It is a wonderful work of the Holy Spirit wrought by the Word upon the saints at their first conversion, whereby corruption of nature is wounded, beloved sins cast away with sorrow, and the sinner received into an everlasting communion with God and his saints. Those that are not thus circumcised are not Israelites, but Ishmaelites; whereas Jether, though by nature an Ishmaelite, {1Ch 2:17} yet, being thus inwardly circumcised, he was, for his faith and religion, called and counted an Israelite. {2Sa 17:25} See Php 3:3-5.
paragraphs.anchor: Circumcise yourselves to the Lord.

paragraphs.text: Not of the flesh only, {see 1Pe 3:21} as the carnal Israelite, who rests in the work done, glorious in outward privileges, neglects the practice of religion and power of godliness, pursueth him that is born after the Spirit, the Israelite indeed, &c., and is therefore disprivileged, hated, and defied by God, as Goliath, that uncircumcised Philistine, was by David, "dead in sins and the uncircumeision of the flesh," {Col 2:13} subject to utter excision, {Gen 17:14} as having no portion in Christ nor in Canaan.
paragraphs.anchor: And take away the foreskin of your heart.

paragraphs.text: Take away therefore the foreskin of the heart; stick not in the bark, pare not off the foreskin of the flesh only, off with the whole "body of sin"; {Col 2:11} begin at Adam’s sin, bewail that; then set upon the beloved sin, out with that eye, off with that hand, "cast away all your transgressions" with as great indignation as angry Zipporah did her child’s foreskin.

Take unto you for this end the sword of the Spirit, the Word, sharper than those stones that she made use of; {Exo 4:25} consider the threats - these will work faith, and that will work fear - apply the promises, {Deu 30:6 Eze 36:26; Eze 36:28} doubt not God’s power, but pray him to thrust his holy hand into your bosoms, and to fetch off the filthy foreskin that is there. Lo, this is the way, walk in it.
When once it hath caught your thorns. {Jer 4:3}
paragraphs.anchor: And burn that none can quench it.

paragraphs.text: As if the prophet should say, I do but lose my labour in calling upon you to mortify your corruptions and to cast away all your transgressions. Uncircumcised ye are in heart and ears, and so will be. Now therefore stand upon your guard against the approaching enemy, and defend yourselves, if at least you are able, from the evil that is coming upon you. Moat up yourselves against God’s fire. {Jer 4:4}
paragraphs.anchor: Declare ye in Judah.

paragraphs.text: All this seemeth to be ironically spoken. {as Jer 4:5}
paragraphs.anchor: Set up the standard towards Zion.

paragraphs.text: i.e., From Babylon. Ab aquilone nihil boni. There is also another Babylon spoken of in the Revelation, which to the true Church hath of long time been lerna malorum; and so the poor persecuted Protestants in Poland feel at this day. Roma radix omnium malorum.
paragraphs.anchor: For I will bring evil from the north

paragraphs.text: i.e., Nebuchadnezzar from Babylon, where he lieth safe, sicut leo in vepreto, and will shortly show himself for a mischief to many people, who shall feel his force and fierceness.
paragraphs.anchor: The lion is come up from his thicket

paragraphs.text: Repent, if at least it be not too late, as the next words hint that now it was.
paragraphs.anchor: For this, gird you with sackcloth.

paragraphs.text: Or, Because the fierce wrath of the Lord will not turn from us; it will have its full forth. See Zep 2:2. {See Trapp on "Zec 2:2"}
paragraphs.anchor: For the fierce wrath of the Lord is not turned back from us.

paragraphs.text: His courage shall be quailed, and he shall be strangely crestfallen. This was fulfilled in Zedekiah, who sought to save himself by flight, but could not.
paragraphs.anchor: The heart of the king shall perish.

paragraphs.text: sc., By those false prophets. {Jer 4:9} Compare 1Ki 18:22-29 Eze 14:9. This God doth as a just judge, punishing sin with sin. The words may be rendered as a question, "Hast thou indeed thus deceived this people?" Is it possible that thou shouldst have an active, or so much as a permissive, hand in such a business?
paragraphs.anchor: Surely thou hast greatly deceived this people

paragraphs.text: i.e., To the heart, it goes as far as it can. Capulo tenus abdidit ensem. See Psa 69:11.
paragraphs.anchor: Whenas the sword reacheth unto the soul

paragraphs.text: Ventus urens et exsiccans, as the north wind is. Understand hereby the King of Babylon, {as Jer 4:6} blasting and wasting all before him.
paragraphs.anchor: A dry wind of the high places.

paragraphs.text: But to dissipate and destroy.
paragraphs.anchor: Not to fan, nor to cleanse.

paragraphs.text: An impetuous and stiff wind, such as shall carry away chaff, and grain, and all.
paragraphs.anchor: Even a full wind from those places.

paragraphs.text: Heb., Utter judgments with them - i.e., I will speak no more by my prophets, but by my judgments.
paragraphs.anchor: Now also will I give sentence against them.

paragraphs.text: Swiftly and numerously.
paragraphs.anchor: Behold, he shall come up as clouds.

paragraphs.text: Which, though the biggest of all fowls, yet fly with greatest speed.
paragraphs.anchor: His horses are swifter than eagles.

paragraphs.text: This he premiseth fitly to his exhortation to repentance; {Jer 4:14} q.d., We are utterly undone, if repentance prevent not.
paragraphs.anchor: Woe unto us, for we are spoiled.

paragraphs.text: “ Currat ergo paenitentia, ne praecurrat sententia. ”

Which defileth it worse than any leprosy, {a} or jakes, doth the body. {Mar 7:19-20; Mar 7:23} Thy hands thou often washest, and other outward parts, placing therein no small religion, thou canst not wash them in innocence; wash them therefore in tears, and when thou hast so done, cry to God with Augustine, Lava lachrymas meas Domine: ipsae enim lachrymae sunt lachrymabiles; Wash my very tears, Lord, for they are lamentable ones. Beg of him to bathe thy soul in the blood of his Son, to wash thee thoroughly from thine iniquity, and to cleanse thee from thy sin. {Psa 51:2}
paragraphs.anchor: O Jerusalem, wash thine heart from wickedness.

paragraphs.text: i.e., Have safety here, and salvation hereafter.
paragraphs.anchor: That thou mayest be saved

paragraphs.text: {b} Heb., In the midst of thee, in the very heart of thee. Creep in they will, but why should they lodge there? why should the devil be at inn with us? be any man’s bedfellow, as he is the angry man’s? {Eph 4:26} David oft "communed with his own heart, and his spirit made diligent search" for such vagrants. {Psa 77:6} Scopabam spiritum meum, {c} so some render it, I swept out my spirit. Carnal hearts are stews of unclean thoughts, slaughter houses of cruel and bloody thoughts, exchanges and shops of vain and vile thoughts, a very forge and mint of false political undermining thoughts, yea, oft a little hell of confused and black imaginations.
paragraphs.anchor: How long shall thy vain thoughts lodge within thee?

paragraphs.text: They had need therefore to be carefully cleansed, and kept with all custody. Grace beginneth at the centre, and from thence goeth to the circumference. God and nature begin at the heart; art begins with the face and outward lineaments; so doth hypocrisy at outward paintings and expressions; it cleanseth the outside of the cup and platter, when the inside is full of ravening and wickedness. {Luk 11:39}
{a} Frustra sunt lavamenta, ubi nulla est innocentia. - Oecol.
{b} Hic mora cogitationis redarguitur et eius adlubescentia. - Oecol.
{c} Vulgate.

Which was first called Laish, then Dan, and after that, in honour of Tiberius Caesar, Caesarea Philippi. {a} It was the utmost bound of Israel northward; and therehence came a rumour of the enemy entering and making his first impression into the land, and so, by Mount Ephraim, to the Jews of Jerusalem. This Jeremiah, by a spirit of prophecy, foretelleth long before, against their vain confidence of better.
paragraphs.anchor: For a voice declareth from Dan.

paragraphs.text: The same Hebrew word signifieth vanity or iniquity in the verse aforegoing. Sin is the mother of misery and molestation.
paragraphs.anchor: And publisheth affliction.

paragraphs.text: {a} Joseph. Antiq., lib. xviii.

i.e., To the Jews, who haply are called the nations, because once better accounted of than all nations. Thus the saints are called "All things," {Col 1:18} and the Rabbis have a saying, that those seventy souls which came down to Egypt with Jacob, were more worth than all the seventy nations of the world besides.
paragraphs.anchor: Make ye mention to the nations

paragraphs.text: Nebuchadnezzar’s body guard, say some. Heb., Notserim - i.e., Nebuchadnezzarenes. {a} Others give a better reason of the word from the next verse.
paragraphs.anchor: That watchers are come.

paragraphs.text: While they invade them cum barritu militari, with a horrid and horrible noise, such as the Turks use today also when they set upon any city to storm it.
paragraphs.anchor: And give out their voice against the cities of Judah.

paragraphs.text: {a} Sicut a Caesare Caesariani, a Praetore Praetoriani.
They have straitly besieged her, so that there is no escaping their hands.
paragraphs.anchor: As keepers of a field, are they against her.

paragraphs.text: This is like as we use to say to our children when they have taken cold or got any harm, This is your gadding and dabbling in the dirt, your going in the snow, your eating of fruit, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: Thy way and thy doings have procured these things unto thee.

paragraphs.text: i.e., Merces malitlae; the wages of thy wickedness, the fruit of thy folly.
paragraphs.anchor: This is thy wickedness

paragraphs.text: Thou hast given God a bitter pill, as it were, that went to his heart; and now he hath given thee as bitter a potion, that reacheth unto thine heart.
paragraphs.anchor: Because it is bitter.

paragraphs.text: So, "My head, my head"; {2Ki 4:19} "My leanness, my leanness." {Isa 24:16} Thus the prophet here, to express his inexpressible grief for the calamities of his people.
paragraphs.anchor: My bowels, my bowels!

paragraphs.text: As a woman in travail; Doleo instar parturientis.
paragraphs.anchor: I am pained.

paragraphs.text: Heb., At the walls of my heart; scil., to see, in spirit, the city walls surprised.
paragraphs.anchor: At the very heart.

paragraphs.text: Saltitat et palpitat, ut in pavidis et perculsis fieri solet, leaps and throbs.
paragraphs.anchor: My heart maketh a noise in me.

paragraphs.text: Heb., I will not.
paragraphs.anchor: I cannot hold my peace.

paragraphs.text: i.e., I have heard in the spirit, and am affected with it, as if already come.
paragraphs.anchor: Because thou hast heard

paragraphs.text: Fluctus fluctum trudit; one mischief upon another, the sword after famine, captivity after a siege.
paragraphs.anchor: Destruction upon destruction.

paragraphs.text: Or, Plundered; which word we first heard of in the Swedish wars.
paragraphs.anchor: For the whole land is spoiled.

paragraphs.text: Sad sights and doleful ditties are common in times of war.
paragraphs.anchor: How long shall I see the standard?

paragraphs.text: Tubam turbamque hostiurn.
paragraphs.anchor: And hear the sound of the trumpet.

paragraphs.text: To know and to worship God aright, is the only true wisdom, saith Lactantius. {a}
paragraphs.anchor: For my people is foolish, they have not known me.

paragraphs.text: In terrenis lyncei, in caelestibus talpae. Wise the wicked are in their generation, subtle and sly; but so is the serpent, or the fox. The swine that wandereth can make better shift to get home than the sheep can to the fold. They have received "the spirit of this world"; {1Co 2:12} the devil also worketh effectually in them, as a smith in his forge. {Eph 2:2} Hence they are "wise to do evil." Elymas was a sorcerer, subtle fellow, but the devil’s child, and so the more dangerous. {Act 13:10} Magnum ingenium et magna tentatio, saith Vincentius Lirinensis, concerning Origen, who had a great wit, but proved a great scandal to the Church. The devil covets to be adorned by thee, said Augustine to one that was wittily wicked. Surely as jet gathereth dross and refuse things to itself, but lets go gold and precious things; so do the world’s wizards.
paragraphs.anchor: They are wise to do evil, but to do good they have no knowledge.

paragraphs.text: {a} Lib. iii. cap. 30.
Tohu vabohit {as Gen 1:2} sightless and shapeless. Sermo est hyperbolicus, all was in a confusion. What shall it, then, be at the last day?
paragraphs.anchor: I beheld the earth, and, lo, it was without form, and void.

paragraphs.text: War is a woe that no words, how wide soever, can sufficiently utter.
paragraphs.anchor: I beheld the mountains, and, lo, they trembled.

paragraphs.text: As being lightened of their burden, saith a Rabbi, trees and houses.
paragraphs.anchor: And all the hills moved lightly.

paragraphs.text: But all killed, captived, or fled. Judaea lay utterly waste for seventy years; insomuch that after the slaughter of Gedaliah, when all, men, women, and children, fled into Egypt, there was not a Jew left in the country.
paragraphs.anchor: I beheld, and, lo, there was no man.

paragraphs.text: Birds were given men for food, medicine, and delight, as companions of his life; therefore it is reckoned, both here and Jer 9:10, as a judgment to lose them.
paragraphs.anchor: And all the birds of the heavens were fled.

paragraphs.text: Who was the chief agent; as Titus the Roman emperor also acknowledged after be had destroyed Jerusalem: Non se id fecisse dixit, sed Deo iram suam declaranti manus suas accommodasse; { a} he said it was not he that had done it, but that he had only lent his hands to God, justly displeased at that nation.
paragraphs.anchor: At the presence of the Lord, &c.

paragraphs.text: {a} Suidas.
God kept the room empty all those seventy years, till the return of the natives.
paragraphs.anchor: Yet I will not make a full end.

paragraphs.text: Quod scrips; scrips, said Pilate, I will not alter it. See the like, Eze 24:13-14.
paragraphs.anchor: Because I have spoken it, &c.

paragraphs.text: See Jer 4:25.
paragraphs.anchor: Every city shall be forsaken.

paragraphs.text: Jezebel-like, {2Ki 9:30 Eze 23:40}
paragraphs.anchor: Though thou rendest thy face with paint.

paragraphs.text: i.e., Seek to ingratiate with the Chaldees, by submitting to them, and worshipping their idols.
paragraphs.anchor: In vain shalt thou make thyself fair

paragraphs.text: As an old withered strumpet, and now out of date. See Eze 16:36; Eze 23:22.
paragraphs.anchor: Thy lovers will despise thee.

paragraphs.text: Primiparae: such have greatest pains, and least patience oft.
paragraphs.anchor: As of her that bringeth forth her first child.

paragraphs.text: Once her paramours, her sweethearts. There is nothing got by comporting with idolaters. The Duke of Medina’s sword knew no difference between Papists and Protestants in 1588, and that they should have found had the Spaniard then prevailed.
paragraphs.anchor: For my soul is wearied because of murderers.
